Summary:
Redwood walked through the regional data handling playbook: how region pinning works, routing/fallback policies, customer-managed KMS options, and the subprocessor map. Zenith's security and legal teams focused on guarantees around EU residency for EU customers, what happens on failover (cross-border processing), audit log granularity, and whether Redwood can support a customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own-kms) or KMS Escrow. Action items captured re: sending SOC2/ISO artifacts, a diagram for region pin flows, and scheduling a KMS deep-dive.

Topics covered:
- Region pinning and geofence behaviors
- Cross-border fallback & acceptable processing zones
- Subprocessor list and EU-based subprocessors
- KMS: customer-managed vs Redwood-managed; HSM/KMS attributes
- Audit logs, retention, and DSAR / data subject requests
- Legal clause language and escalation process

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have most folks on, we're going to run through our regional data handling playbook and answer any q's on residency and kms, um, if we can hold questions until the end we'll make sure we capture them, but feel free to interrupt.
[00:10] Marta Ruiz: thanks Lena, yeah quick context — we operate in EU and US, regulators expect EU-resident PII to remain in eu land, that's the big blocker for us. We're also evaluating vendors for dedicated capacity for inference.
[00:20] Marco Nguyen: great, quick intro — I'm Marco, I handle architecture and infra for Redwood's private and dedicated offerings, I built the region-pin routing logic. I'll show slides then an architecture sketch.
[00:35] Priya Sinha: just to flag, legal will want explicit language about "no cross-border exfil unless auth'd" and a process for DSARs.
[00:45] Alan Cho: and from infra side we want to know whether we can bring our KMS — like a customer-managed key in our AWS account — and how tokenization or cache might leave the eu.
[00:58] Lena Park: totally — we'll cover both, Marco will show the primary + fallback flows. high level, region pinning means requests from eu users can be routed to eu-hosted nodes; we maintain a subprocessor inventory and have an option to limit processing to region, or to allow fallback to us regions under strict conditions.
[01:20] Marco Nguyen: jumping in — diagram, if you think about request routing there's a policy layer that looks at customer config: pin_region = eu-west-1, allow_fallback = false/true, strict_residency boolean. If strict_residency=true, we will reject requests when no eu capacity is available. if allow_fallback=true, requests will failover to the next region that meets compliance constraints — and that might be us-east-1 for global customers.
[01:48] Marta Ruiz: ok that helps, but what about background tasks? like model cache prefetching or KV cache warmers, do those happen cross-region?
[01:58] Marco Nguyen: good question — we try to co-locate KV cache with the serving runtime. for Dedicated and Private deployments it's customer-configurable; for Hosted we default to region-local caches. There are cases where long-running batch jobs or model refreshes might touch global storage; those are controlled and logged.
[02:18] Priya Sinha: can you clarify "controlled and logged" — we need audit trail that shows which region touched what PII and timestamps, ideally immutable logs for compliance.
[02:28] Lena Park: yes, we provide audit logs with request id, model, timestamp, serving node region, and whether KMS wrap/unwrap happened. we retain logs per customer retention policy; for enterprise plans we can extend retention and provide S3 export.
[02:40] Alan Cho: and what's the fidelity — do logs include KV cache hits vs misses? can we tie a token generation to a specific node?
[02:50] Marco Nguyen: current logs capture request routing and cache hit/miss at a per-request level. we can emit additional context headers or fields on request metadata if you need deeper traceability.
[03:05] Marta Ruiz: about subprocessors — many vendors list dozens; we need to know which subprocessors are in eu and which have access to keys or raw logs.
[03:15] Lena Park: we maintain a subprocessor inventory and will share the current CSV. most infra subprocessors are cloud providers and logging providers — we have EU-based storage and compute subprocessors for our eu region. any subprocessor access to cleartext PII is restricted and recorded.
[03:30] Priya Sinha: on KMS — can Redwood support customer-managed KMS where key material never leaves our HSM? or do you always perform wrap/unwrap?
[03:40] Marco Nguyen: for Hosted we support a few modes: Redwood-managed keys, customer-provided keys (where you upload a key to Redwood's KMS integration), and a bring-your-own-kms flow where you hold the root in your cloud account and we call your KMS via a cross-account role for wrap/unwrap. In the strictest mode, sensitive data is encrypted with your key and we store only ciphertext. We also support HSM-backed KMS options with FIPS modules.
[04:08] Alan Cho: cross-account calls are fine, but we worry about network latencies. does Redwood cache plaintext to avoid repeat unwraps?
[04:18] Marco Nguyen: we try not to cache plaintext. we use envelope encryption patterns: data encrypted with a per-request ephemeral key, that key wrapped by the customer key. we maintain an encrypted KV; only the runtime performing inference can unwrap the ephemeral key, and we avoid persistent plaintext caching. there are short-lived in-memory caches for performance but they're ephemeral and TTL-limited.
[04:45] Marta Ruiz: what about failover behavior — if eu nodes go down and allow_fallback=true, do we copy data to us nodes or just process in-place?
[04:55] Marco Nguyen: if allow_fallback=true, incoming requests are routed to the fallback region and the processing happens there; that means there is cross-border processing. we can optionally anonymize or strip PII before failover, or request a manual approval flow. if strict_residency=true we will reject rather than failover.
[05:15] Priya Sinha: manual approval flow? that's operationally heavy, but could work for sensitive classes. is there a UI/console control?
[05:22] Lena Park: yes, in the Console you can set routing policies per environment and per model, and you can set rules based on data sensitivity tags. we also support canary rollouts where a percent of requests may be allowed to failover for testing.
[05:35] Alan Cho: we also want to ensure that model artifacts (weights) are not replicated cross-region unless agreed.
[05:42] Marco Nguyen: model weights are treated as code/artifact; by default a model variant is uploaded per-region for residency-required customers. for hosted multi-region models we can provide region-isolated model stores.
[05:55] Marta Ruiz: certificate and attestation question — do you have SOC 2 type II and ISO 27001? and can you provide penetration test summaries?
[06:02] Lena Park: yes we have SOC 2 type II and ISO 27001; we'll share the certs and a sanitized pentest summary (with NDAs if requested). link to our public security page is: https://redwood.example.com/security — we'll attach the artifacts.
[06:20] Priya Sinha: legal question — indemnity/risk allocation around accidental cross-border processing — is that in standard agreement or negotiable?
[06:28] Lena Park: we have enterprise clauses — most teams want measurable SLAs and agreed-upon remedies; it's negotiable for dedicated/private deals. we'll flag legal and bring standard language for your review.
[06:40] Alan Cho: on subprocessors again, clarify whether any subprocessor has access to unencrypted logs or keys.
[06:48] Marco Nguyen: subprocessors do not have access to raw keys. some subprocessors process telemetry or aggregate logs; we segregate those and scrub PII where possible. any need to give subprocessor access to plaintext requires an explicit contract and is rare.
[07:05] Marta Ruiz: if we choose dedicated capacity in eu, are there any subprocessors outside eu?
[07:12] Lena Park: for Dedicated we can run on eu-only subprocessors for compute and storage; our inventory will show EU-based options. some monitoring vendors are global, but we can swap to EU-only providers on enterprise deals.
[07:25] Priya Sinha: retention of logs and exports — can we get daily push of audit logs to our S3 in eu?
[07:32] Marco Nguyen: yes, S3 exports in customer buckets are supported; we can push logs to your eu bucket via cross-account role. retention policies are configurable.
[07:45] Alan Cho: can we get a short live demo of the config in the Console where you toggle strict_residency?
[07:51] Lena Park: we can do that but maybe as a follow-up; this call is heavy on legal and architecture. we'll schedule the demo for Marco to show the Console toggles and the routing behavior.
[08:05] Marta Ruiz: one more — DSAR processing: if a data subject requests deletion, what's Redwood's role vs Zenith?
[08:13] Marco Nguyen: typically Redwood acts as a processor; requests should flow via Zenith to Redwood. we provide APIs to search raw logs/requests and delete per retention policy. for Hosted we can purge request-level artifacts; for Dedicated/Private it's often customer-managed.
[08:30] Priya Sinha: ok that's good, we want a written runbook for DSARs.
[08:35] Lena Park: we'll add a runbook template to the docs and include contact points.
[08:40] Marta Ruiz: do you do subprocessor SOC audits?
[08:43] Marco Nguyen: we require subprocessors to have at least industry-standard certifications where applicable; we also do vendor risk assessments for higher privilege subprocessors.
[08:55] Alan Cho: question: is there any scenario where PII is included in model embeddings stored on a global vector DB?
[09:03] Marco Nguyen: embeddings are cached per-customer and region; for high-sensitivity customers we recommend encryption + region isolation; we also support ephemeral embeddings that are not written to long-term storage.
[09:18] Priya Sinha: legal follow-up: please provide sample contract language for data residency and breach notification timelines.
[09:25] Lena Park: yes we'll include sample contract clauses.
[09:28] Marta Ruiz: side note — do you list subprocessors with their country and their access level? that's what regulators ask for.
[09:35] Lena Park: yes the CSV includes name, country, function, and whether they have access to plaintext.
[09:42] Alan Cho: on KMS again, any latency considerations when using customer KMS in eu-west-1 for wrap/unwrap?
[09:50] Marco Nguyen: extra RTTs for wrap/unwrap — we do envelope keys to minimize KMS calls. recommended pattern is to keep the customer KMS in the same region as compute to reduce latency.
[10:02] Marta Ruiz: would you support a policy of pre-approved fallback destinations? like we only allow failover to other eu territories (e.g., eu-central) but never to the us?
[10:12] Marco Nguyen: yes, routing policy supports allowed_fallback_regions list; you can enumerate allowed regions and we will only route within that set.
[10:22] Priya Sinha: and audits — can we get periodic attestation that no cross-border processing occurred for a given timeframe?
[10:29] Lena Park: we can provide a signed attestation for an agreed window and filtering criteria; that's a standard enterprise deliverable.
[10:38] Alan Cho: curious about edge cases — what happens to async tasks queued during outage? are they backfilled cross-region?
[10:46] Marco Nguyen: async queues are region-scoped by default. if you enable cross-region recovery, the queue may be replayed in fallback region — again configurable.
[10:55] Marta Ruiz: this is helpful, I think next steps are artifacts and a diagram. one more ask: can Redwood provide a short runbook for incident escalation specifically about unintended cross-border processing?
[11:05] Lena Park: yes, we'll draft an incident escalation runbook and include points for notification timelines and remediation steps.
[11:12] Priya Sinha: legal will look at the indemnity language once we see the attestation and the contract sample.
[11:18] Lena Park: perfect. recap of next steps: we'll send SOC2 and ISO, subprocessor CSV, region-pin diagram, schedule KMS deep-dive and a Console demo.
[11:30] Marta Ruiz: thanks everyone, that's it from me.
[11:34] Alan Cho: thanks — looking forward to the KMS session.
[11:36] Marco Nguyen: thanks all, I'll share the diagram and a short tech note on envelope encryption pattern.
[11:40] Lena Park: thanks — we'll follow up by email with links and the artifacts noted.
[11:48] (call ends)
